A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
in cases of acute SAH from a vertebral artery anurysm, a more aggressive management with PED alone may be considered.
in patients with a ruptured vertebrobasillar fusiform aneurism with an associated SAH, the use of flow diverting stents may be associated with a higher risk for aneurysm growth and rebleeding.
in cases with SAH from fusiform aneurysl lesions, the use of flow diversion should be reserved only for cases in which there is no other viable alternative and the patient is hemodynamically stable.
The main takeaway from our work is that
in cases with aneurysms with complex morphology and in patients with a history of SAH, a more aggressive treatment strategy with the use of flow diverters should be adopted.
in cases where flow diversion devices are used for the treatment of SAH from a complex vertebrobasillar aneurysm, a close follow-up is warranted to detect any signs of persistent aneurismal growth.
in the setting of acute subarachoid hemorrhage from a fusiform aneurism of the posterior circulation, coiling with or without the PED is not the treatment of choice.
